GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg|brace-expansion.notes: brace-expansion DoS via unbounded expansion length. REWRITTEN 2026-08-05 (§2.129); the previous note's conclusion was wrong. It claimed upstream 'backported nothing to the 1.x/2.x lines' and that the only exit was migrating eslint 8 -> 10. Upstream has since shipped 1.1.18, 2.1.4 and 5.0.9, so the per-major `overrides` in package.json pin every line, and the twenty advisory paths that note enumerated (eslint, @typescript-eslint, the electron-builder packaging chain, @sentry/vite-plugin, test-exclude) are ALL GONE. One node remains: `node_modules/npm/node_modules/brace-expansion`, marked `dev: true` and `inBundle: true` — the copy vendored inside the npm CLI that the `@semantic-release/npm` devDependency pulls in. npm declares 65 bundleDependencies, so a child `overrides` entry cannot reach inside the bundle. THE NPM 12 EXIT IS DISPROVEN — DO NOT RETRY IT. This note used to claim that overriding the top-level `npm` dependency to 12.0.2 'would clear it', deferred only as an unwanted major bump. That was written from reasoning, never tested. It was tested on 2026-08-24: `overrides: { npm: ^12.0.2 }` installs npm 12.0.2 and the SAME advisories persist on the SAME node, because npm 12.0.2 still bundles brace-expansion 5.0.7 (vulnerable range 4.0.0-5.0.8), ip-address 10.2.0 (vulnerable <=10.3.0) and tar 7.5.19 (vulnerable <=7.5.20). npm's declared ranges (e.g. `tar: ^7.5.19`) do not describe the bundle: what ships inside the tarball is whatever was resolved when npm itself was published, and a permissive range proves nothing about it. The override was reverted. Anyone re-reading this: verify the bundled versions on disk under `node_modules/npm/node_modules/` before believing any claim about which npm release fixes what. Unreachability rests on `dev` + `inBundle` + absence from the shipped bundle, NOT on `npm run audit:prod` — that script excludes devDependencies, and `undici` shows why it is no proof of shipped safety: it is a devDependency that vite bundles into the main process, so `audit:prod` does not cover code we actually ship. SCOPE, stated honestly: the key is package-scoped rather than chain-scoped because npm's v3 audit output gives nodes, not dependency chains, and audit-ci can only narrow to the package name. A FUTURE runtime path of brace-expansion would therefore also be suppressed until expiry; the 2026-11-01 date is the backstop that forces a re-look. Exit conditions: @semantic-release/npm moves off a vendored npm, or we take the npm 12 override.

GHSA-r292-9mhp-454m|npm>tar.notes: CVE-2026-73566, tar <= 7.5.20: `mapHas` inside `filesFilter` recurses without a depth bound, so an archive whose entry paths carry tens of thousands of segments exhausts the call stack and kills the process. High, CVSS 7.5, fixed upstream in 7.5.21. Published to the registry after 2026-08-22 — the pipeline went red with no dependency change on our side, exactly as GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895 did before it. ONE node, and it is the same one as every other entry in this file: `node_modules/npm/node_modules/tar`, `dev: true`, `inBundle: true` — the copy vendored inside the npm CLI that the `@semantic-release/npm` devDependency carries. npm declares its bundleDependencies, so an `overrides` entry cannot reach inside the bundle; audit's own `fixAvailable` proposes @semantic-release/npm 12.0.2, which is a MAJOR DOWNGRADE from the 13.x we run, not a fix. REACHABILITY: to be exploited this needs the vendored npm to extract an attacker-supplied tarball WITH member selection, during a release run, on our own runner — release tooling that never reaches a user's machine and never touches mail. Unreachability rests on `dev` + `inBundle` + absence from the shipped bundle, NOT on `npm run audit:prod` (see the brace-expansion note for why that script proves nothing about shipped code). SCOPE, and here it is NARROWER than the entries above: audit-ci emitted a full chain for this one, so the key pins `semantic-release>@semantic-release/npm>npm>tar` rather than the bare package name. A future runtime path of tar therefore still fails the build instead of being silently covered — which is what the package-scoped keys above regret and could not avoid. The 2026-11-01 expiry is a backstop that forces a re-look, not a renewal. Exit conditions: @semantic-release/npm moves off a vendored npm, or we take the npm 12 override, or the vendored npm ships tar 7.5.21. KEY SHORTENED 2026-08-27, and the paragraph above predicted exactly this: the key was `semantic-release>@semantic-release/npm>npm>tar` and audit-ci now derives `npm>tar` for the same finding, so the pipeline went red on develop with no dependency change on our side (pipeline 2476). Re-verified before editing, on disk rather than from the report: still ONE node `node_modules/npm/node_modules/tar`, `isDirect: false`, `effects: ['npm']`, vendored tar 7.5.19 inside npm 11.18.0, `tar` listed in npm's own `bundleDependencies`, and `npm` is neither a dependency nor a devDependency nor an override of ours. Nothing about reachability moved; only the chain audit-ci prints did. The new key is one level less specific but is NOT the bare package name: a path audit-ci emits differently — `mailparser>tar`, `foo>npm>tar`, or a bare `tar` — does not match `npm>tar` and still fails the build, which is most of the property the previous author chose this scoping for. State the limit precisely, because the earlier draft of this sentence overstated it and codex-security-review caught that on 2026-08-27: audit-ci matches the path it PRINTS, not the provenance behind it, so what is no longer enforced is ancestry above `npm`. If a future runtime route ever gets coalesced into the same printed `npm>tar`, this entry would suppress it silently. Restoring the old provenance guarantee is not a matter of picking a better key — no key can, since audit-ci no longer emits that ancestry — it would take a separate CI assertion over the audit node data. Practical warning for whoever meets this next: the chain audit-ci emits is derived from `npm audit`'s `effects` graph, not from our lockfile, so it can change under us again on any advisory-database update. A chain-scoped key buys precision at the cost of this fragility; that trade was made deliberately and is being kept, not regretted.

GHSA-mwp4-54f8-5fhr|ip-address.notes: ip-address: Address4 decodes leading-zero octets as decimal while resolvers decode them as octal, allowing SSRF and trust-boundary bypass. THE PATH THAT MATTERED IS FIXED, NOT SUPPRESSED: `imapflow -> socks -> ip-address` is shipped code and now resolves to 10.4.0 through the overrides block. Suppressing it there would have hollowed out this project's SSRF posture (`safeRemoteFetch`, CLAUDE.md §5), which is the opposite of what an allowlist is for. What is allowlisted is one leftover node, `node_modules/npm/node_modules/ip-address`, marked `dev: true` and `inBundle: true`, inside the npm CLI vendored by the `@semantic-release/npm` devDependency — release tooling absent from the shipped application. As above, deferred rather than unfixable: a top-level npm 12 override would clear it. Same package-scoped-key caveat: a future runtime path of ip-address would also be suppressed until the 2026-11-01 expiry, so re-triage then rather than renewing blind.
